title: Tenant isolation, auth flows and subdomain portals: a sample architecture for Collabify
summary: A sample walkthrough of how a shared Postgres schema with row level security, subdomain client portals, multiple auth flows and large video uploads could fit together. All data shown is sample data.

scenes.heading: Request path from subdomain to isolated data
scenes.caption: Shows how a request on a client subdomain is resolved to a tenant and kept inside that tenant's rows.

steps.label: Request hits acme.example.com
steps.detail: Next.js middleware reads the host header and extracts the subdomain slug.
steps.on_error: Unknown subdomain returns a generic not-found page, with no hint whether the tenant exists.

steps.label: Resolve slug to tenant
steps.detail: Look up the tenant id from a small tenants table, cached briefly at the edge.
steps.on_error: If the lookup fails, the request is rejected rather than served without a tenant.

steps.label: Authenticate the user
steps.detail: Session or token is verified and checked to belong to the resolved tenant.
steps.on_error: Mismatch between user tenant and subdomain tenant ends the session and redirects to sign-in.

steps.label: Set tenant context in Postgres
steps.detail: Each transaction sets the tenant id and role as a local setting before any query runs.
steps.on_error: If the setting is missing, the RLS policies match no rows, so the query returns nothing.

steps.label: RLS policies filter every query
steps.detail: Policies compare each row's tenant_id to the transaction's tenant setting.
steps.on_error: A policy violation on write raises an error and the transaction rolls back.

steps.label: Render the client portal
steps.detail: The portal shows only that tenant's projects, files and members.

scenes.heading: Row level security on a shared schema
scenes.caption: A short sample of the policy pattern that keeps tenants apart on one set of tables.

scenes.heading: Sample tenant isolation test matrix
scenes.caption: Shows the kind of checks that would run in CI to prove one tenant can never read or write another's data.

scenes.heading: Large video upload pipeline
scenes.caption: Shows one way to take big video files from a client portal into storage without tying up the app server.

steps.label: Portal requests an upload
steps.detail: The API checks the user's tenant and quota, then creates an upload record scoped to that tenant.

steps.label: Issue signed multipart URLs
steps.detail: The browser uploads parts straight to object storage under a tenant-prefixed path.
steps.on_error: A failed part is retried on its own; the upload resumes instead of restarting.

steps.label: Complete and verify
steps.detail: The API confirms all parts, checks size and content type, and marks the file ready.
steps.on_error: Incomplete or oversized uploads are flagged and cleaned up by a scheduled job.

steps.label: Process in the background
steps.detail: A queued job handles any transcoding or thumbnails and writes status back to the file row.
steps.on_error: Failed jobs retry with backoff, then show a clear failed state to the client.

assumptions: Assumed object storage with signed multipart uploads for video; the post does not name a storage provider.
Assumed the app connects to Postgres through a role without BYPASSRLS so policies always apply.
Assumed tenant is resolved from the subdomain, with a custom domain option left open.
Assumed the multiple auth flows include at least email sign-in for client users and a separate staff login; the post does not specify them.
Assumed background jobs run on a queue; the post names no specific tool.
Table and policy names are sample names, not Collabify's real schema.
